title: Restaurant POS Buying Checklist: 10 Tests Before You Purchase
subtitle: An operational evaluation framework for restaurant owners. Test order flow, printer routing, billing accuracy, and support before signing a contract.
excerpt: Use this 10-point restaurant POS buying checklist to test order entry, kitchen routing, billing, devices, support and contract terms during a product demonstration.

tableOfContents.title: Why you need a hands-on buying checklist
Test 1: Order entry speed during rush hour
Test 2: Multi-station KOT routing and amendments
Test 3: Offline resilience when the internet drops
Test 4: Split billing, discounts, and payment methods
Test 5: Visual table management and status updates
Test 7: Cash drawer reconciliations and shift audits
Test 8: Hardware compatibility and printer setup
Test 10: Renewal costs, data ownership, and support SLAs

sections.heading: Why you need a hands-on buying checklist
paragraphs: A POS demonstration can show order entry, kitchen handoff and checkout in one session. Test it with a menu and service conditions that match your restaurant, including several staff entering orders, a printer running low on paper and a guest changing an item after it reaches the kitchen.

Use the same service conditions to compare restaurant management software. To identify the best POS for restaurant operations, test ten workflows against your own service, note the steps involved and ask how each system handles failures before comparing contract terms.

callout.title: Run the demo yourself
callout.text: Ask for access to the demo software. Enter an eight-item order with custom spice modifications, split the bill three ways and note the steps for each action. Ask the representative to show how the same order is handled if a device or connection fails.

sections.heading: Test 1: Order entry speed during rush hour
paragraphs: The first verification step on your restaurant pos buying checklist focuses on order punching speed. In a busy dining room or quick-service counter, every additional click slows down service. A waiter taking an order on a tablet or a counter cashier punching orders during a lunch rush should be able to select dishes, specify variants (such as Half or Full), and send the order to the kitchen within thirty seconds.

When evaluating a restaurant pos system, test the search and navigation speed. Can staff search by dish name, item code, or category tab? Can they add frequent notes such as less spicy or no garlic with one tap, or do they have to open a nested modal dialog?

sections.heading: Test 2: Multi-station KOT routing and amendments
paragraphs: A full-service restaurant needs its point of sale software to split an order across kitchen departments automatically. Ask the sales team to configure two distinct kitchen stations (such as Tandoor and Main Kitchen) plus a beverage bar.

Enter an order containing starters, main curries, and mocktails. Confirm that the software splits the ticket correctly. Next, test an amendment: add two more garlic naans and cancel one starter. Observe whether the kitchen printer prints a clear amendment slip that flags the cancellation to the chef.

sections.heading: Test 3: Offline resilience when the internet drops
paragraphs: Ask the vendor to explain what each part of the system requires during an internet interruption. Order entry, kitchen printing, bill preparation, payment recording and cloud reports may behave differently, so request the limits and recovery process for each workflow.

With the representative's permission, interrupt the connection during a demo. Record which actions continue, which pause, whether orders queue, and how the system handles reconnection. Confirm the documented behavior for the exact devices and network setup you plan to use.

sections.heading: Test 4: Split billing, discounts, and payment methods
paragraphs: Checkout is where guest friction peaks. Split billing verification forms the fourth checkpoint on this restaurant pos buying checklist. Your restaurant billing system must handle common customer payment requests without calling a senior manager to override the screen every time.
Test these four scenarios on the demo terminal:

checklist.detail: A party of four wants to divide the check based on who ordered what, separating appetizers from drinks.
Splitting a ₹4,200 total equally across three separate credit cards or UPI scans.
Recording ₹1,000 in cash and ₹1,450 via UPI QR on the same invoice.
Applying an authorized percentage discount with an audit note explaining the reason.

sections.heading: Test 5: Visual table management and status updates
paragraphs: Front-of-house staff need a clear visual map of the dining floor. Floor views should display table numbers, current seating status, party size, and elapsed dining time.
Verify that staff can transfer a seated party from Table T2 to Table T6 if the air conditioning is too cold, carrying the open order and running KOTs over seamlessly without voiding items.

sections.heading: Test 6: Instant 86ing and menu editing
paragraphs: When the kitchen runs out of fresh fish at 9:00 PM, servers must know immediately so they do not take orders for sold-out items (known in restaurant parlance as 86ing an item).

Test how long it takes a floor manager to mark an item unavailable. Does the toggle reflect immediately on every waiter handheld and counter POS terminal, or does it require restarting the application?

sections.heading: Test 7: Cash drawer reconciliations and shift audits
paragraphs: Cash discrepancies occur during shift handoffs when cashiers change duties between lunch and dinner. Cashier shift control is the seventh verification item on this restaurant pos buying checklist. A reliable restaurant POS system provides opening cash float declarations, mid-shift petty cash recordings, and end-of-shift blind closes.
Check whether cashiers can close their shifts by counting the physical cash drawer before the system reveals expected totals. This blind close practice prevents cashiers from pocketing excess cash.

sections.heading: Test 8: Hardware compatibility and printer setup
paragraphs: List the device models, operating systems and printer models you plan to use, then ask the vendor to confirm compatibility for each one. Include connection type, setup responsibility, replacement options and any hardware or support charges in the written proposal.

Test receipt printing from the actual device and printer setup where possible. Check the print layout, duplicate handling, connection recovery and the support process when a printer becomes unavailable.

sections.heading: Test 9: Multi-outlet centralized reporting
paragraphs: If you operate or plan to open a second restaurant branch, managing separate menus and reports for each outlet creates administrative overhead. Look for software that supports centralized master menu creation with outlet-level price overrides, and group-level consolidated sales reporting.

sections.heading: Test 10: Renewal costs, data ownership, and support SLAs
paragraphs: The final section of your restaurant pos buying checklist examines the commercial contract. Software costs extend beyond the first-year purchase price. Review contract fine print before paying an advance. Essential contractual questions include:

checklist.detail: Will the subscription fee increase by 30% or 50% at year two renewal?
Does the vendor provide telephone support during Friday and Saturday dinner service, or only email tickets during weekday banking hours?
Can you export your full sales history, customer records, and menu items to CSV or Excel if you choose to switch vendors in the future?

faqs.question: How should an operator use this restaurant pos buying checklist during a demonstration?
faqs.answer: Print or review the checklist before the call. Request access to the demo software, enter realistic test orders, simulate an offline internet disconnection, and test a split bill before discussing contractual pricing.

faqs.question: What is the most important feature to test during a restaurant POS demo?
faqs.answer: Test offline reliability and order-to-kitchen printing. A restaurant can survive a slow report, but it cannot operate if orders cannot reach the kitchen or bills cannot be generated during internet outages.

faqs.question: Should a small restaurant buy a cloud POS or a local server POS?
faqs.answer: There is no single setup for every restaurant. Compare which workflows require a connection, what continues during an outage, how queued transactions are reconciled, and how each option fits your network and support needs.

faqs.question: How long does it take to train restaurant staff on a new POS?
faqs.answer: Run floor and cashier staff through the order, kitchen handoff, payment and shift tasks they will use during service. Ask for the training plan and check that each role can complete its work.

faqs.question: Are proprietary POS hardware terminals mandatory?
faqs.answer: Ask the provider for the supported devices, operating systems, printer models and connection types. Confirm compatibility and setup requirements in writing before choosing hardware.
